title_original: 50 films to watch this awards season
excerpt_original: Voting opens for the early rounds of Bafta and Oscar very soon. Screen International presents its guide to titles likely to engage attention.

blocks.alt: [Clockwise from left] 'Being Heumann', 'The Odyssey', 'Behemoth!', 'Wild Horse Nine', 'Possible Love', 'La Bola Negra', 'Godzilla Minus Zero'

blocks.text: Source: Apple TV / Universal / Searchlight Pictures / Netflix / Elastica / Toho
[Clockwise from left] ‘Being Heumann’, ‘The Odyssey’, ‘Behemoth!’, ‘Wild Horse Nine’, ‘Possible Love’, ‘La Bola Negra’, ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’

Voters for the Bafta Film Awards and US Academy Awards must be in no doubt that awards season is in full swing: the pace of screening invites has stepped up; new titles are landing daily on the academy viewing portals; and talent Q&A events are proliferating.

Just a few days before this edition went to press, Bafta published its viewing groups for voters, revealing there are 224 features vying for attention this year, including 68 documentaries. The time to concentrate minds is truly upon us, with round one Bafta voting opening on December 4 (yes, so soon!), and voting for the 12 Oscar categories that benefit from a shortlist stage running December 7-11. You’ll be forgiven for already feeling daunted by the task ahead.

Screen International’ s special editions for awards voters begin with our annual overview of films in contention for Oscars and Baftas in key categories – from the US, UK and across the world, and including live-action, animation and non-­fiction. Below is also a round-up of the eye-catching performances for voters to watch, and over the coming days Screen will publish separate listings for UK indies and documentaries. Of course, we are not suggesting that viewing should be limited to our selections, and Screen ’s intention is always to expand the awards conversation, not narrow it.

Last year, Paul Thomas Anderson’s September-released One Battle After Another established itself as an early awards front-runner, ultimately scooping best film at Bafta and best picture at Oscar, plus a hefty haul across the categories. Strong competition came from the likes of Sinners , Hamnet , Marty Supreme and Sentimental Value .

This year, studio blockbusters including Project Hail Mary and The Odyssey look set to compete with festival-launched films including Cannes breakout La Bola Negra and a slew of voter-friendly titles landing in the autumn. Entries as diverse as horror hybrid Obsession , sex comedy The Invite and meta-documentary You Can See Everything will seek to broaden the scope of awards contenders, battling with an array of prestige dramas. We wish you an enjoyable – and inspiring – cinematic immersion.
Charles Gant, Awards/box office editor

All Of A Sudden Dir. Ryusuke Hamaguchi Virginie Efira and Tao Okamoto shared the best actress prize at Cannes for this France and Japan-set three-hour-plus drama about strangers who meet in Paris and form a close bond; now it is Japan’s contender for the international feature Oscar. Director and co-writer Hamaguchi will be familiar to voters: Drive My Car became the first Japanese film nominated for a best picture Oscar in 2022, and it won the international film categories at both the Academy Awards and Bafta Film Awards. Neon releases All Of A Sudden in the US on November 25, with Curzon in the UK in February.

Artificial Dir. Luca Guadagnino Working from an original screenplay by former Saturday Night Live writer Simon Rich, this biographical drama tells the story of OpenAI, laying out a clash of ethics between chief scientific officer Ilya Sutskever ( Anora ’s Yura Borisov) and charismatic CEO Sam Altman (Andrew Garfield). Guadagnino’s Call Me By Your Name earned four nominations each at Oscar and Bafta in 2018, winning in both cases for James Ivory’s adapted screenplay. Tech business is a dominant theme for film this year: The Social Reckoning and documentaries Musk and You Can See Everything are also in the mix.

Behemoth! Dir. Tony Gilroy Pedro Pascal is receiving significant buzz for his role as a studio session cellist at a personal crossroads. This Searchlight Pictures drama, which opens in the US on December 4 after debuting at New York Film Festival, is the first feature from writer/director Gilroy in 14 years. His 2007 thriller Michael Clayton earned him Oscar nominations for director and original screenplay, and a Bafta screenplay nod. Gilroy incorporated the work of nine different composers to create the varied scores played by Pascal’s cellist, including contributions from Oscar and Bafta winner Michael Giacchino (Pixar’s Up ).

Being Heumann Dir. Sian Heder CODA provided the underdog-­triumph story of awards season in 2022, scooping Oscars for picture, adapted screenplay (for Heder) and supporting actor for Troy Kotsur. The filmmaker is back in contention with this Toronto-launched Apple Studios biographical drama, adapting Judith Heumann’s memoir to show how the disability activist (Ruth Madeley) led a 1977 San Francisco sit-in protest that ultimately forced the US government to pay more than lip service to disability rights. Four-time Oscar nominee Mark Ruffalo plays her beleaguered adversary in the Jimmy Carter administration.

The Beloved Dir. Rodrigo Sorogoyen Although not selected as Spain’s international feature Oscar entry, this Cannes Competition title is in the awards conversation propelled by Javier Bardem’s lead performance. The actor plays an acclaimed film director who returns to his native Spain after 15 years and casts his estranged daughter (Victoria Luengo) in his next project — but the shoot on the Canary Islands goes far from smoothly. Kino Lorber is giving The Beloved an awards-qualifying release in the US in late 2026, before a wider early 2027 theatrical rollout. Sorogoyen’s 2022 film The Beasts won multiple Goya Awards and a César for best foreign film.

Bunker Dir. Florian Zeller Javier Bardem and Penelope Cruz — both Oscar and Bafta winners in supporting categories respectively for No Country For Old Men and Vicky Cristina Barcelona — star in this London-set psychological drama. Writer/director Zeller had Oscar and Bafta success with The Father in 2021, winning adapted screenplay at both, and each also delivering actor prizes to Anthony Hopkins. This is Zeller’s first original screenplay, although he takes acknowledged inspiration from 2010 Argentinian film The Man Next Door . Sony Pictures Classics’ US awards-qualifying run is in December, with Studio­canal to follow in the UK in February.

Clarissa Dirs. Arie Esiri, Chuko Esiri Twin brothers Arie and Chuko Esiri adapted Virginia Woolf’s 1925 novel Mrs Dalloway , setting the action in modern-day Lagos with flashbacks to an earlier timeframe. Debuting in Directors’ Fortnight at Cannes, Clarissa is the Nigerian filmmakers’ second feature, following 2020 Berlin premiere This Is My Desire ( Eyimofe ). The Neon release stars Sophie Okonedo, David Oyelowo and Toheeb Jimoh, who is perhaps best known for his Primetime Emmy-nominated breakthrough in Ted Lasso . Okonedo has been nominated three time for a Bafta TV award — most recently in Criminal: UK — and received an Oscar nod in 2005 for Hotel Rwanda .
Source: A24
‘Club Kid’

Club Kid Dir. Jordan Firstman Club Kid was the focus of a frenzied bidding war after its Cannes’ Un Certain Regard premiere, eventually won by A24, and the heat has carried on through festival plays at Telluride, Toronto, BFI London and San Sebastian. Its opening weekend North American box office was $403,000 from six sites. Actor Firstman ( I Love LA ) stars in his feature directing debut as a New York queer club promoter brought out of a dark spiral by the arrival of a British son (Reggie Absolom) he never knew existed. The cast also includes Cara Delevingne, Diego Calva and Eldar Isgandarov, who is also in The Debut .

The Debut Dir. Jesse Eisenberg Julianne Moore could take home her second Academy Award and second Bafta for her acclaimed role in writer/director Eisenberg’s A24 comedy about a timid housewife who joins a small-town musical theatre production. Playing the show’s beleaguered director, Paul Giamatti has garnered his best reviews since he collected Oscar and Bafta nominations in 2024 for The Holdovers . Eisenberg won the 2025 original screenplay Bafta for A Real Pain , and voters may appreciate the fact he not only wrote The Debut but also the musical numbers in the film’s fictitious stage show Nosy Neighbors . Lionsgate releases in the UK.

Digger Dir. Alejandro G Iñárritu Wildly anticipated at the start of awards season, and drawing polarised responses since its September launch, Iñárritu’s lavishly budgeted satirical meta comedy has drawn some passionate fans urging voters to tune out the negative sentiment, weak critics scores and disappointing box office ($50m worldwide). The film’s best chances may be in craft categories, including Emmanuel Lubezki’s cinematography, Dennis Gassner and Richard Johnson’s production design, and make-up and hair including prosthetics for Tom Cruise and Riz Ahmed created by two-time Oscar winner Kazu Hiro.

The Drama Dir. Kristoffer Borgli Norway’s Borgli built a cult following with Sick Of Myself (2022) and Dream Scenario (2023), before breaking through into the mainstream with A24 dark comedy The Drama — propelled to $135m global box office with the help of lead actors Zendaya and Robert Pattinson as an engaged couple in total meltdown. Both have a shot at lead acting nominations, but their stronger chances may lie elsewhere this season: Primetime for Pattinson and Dune: Part Three for Zendaya. Nominations so far for The Drama include the audience award category at the Gothams.

Dune: Part Three Dir. Denis Villeneuve Dune won six Oscars and five Baftas in craft categories in 2022, while Part Two nabbed two apiece for sound and visual effects in 2025. Can concluding chapter Part Three follow The Lord Of The Rings playbook, which saw The Return Of The King effect an Oscars sweep in 2004, essentially as reward for the trilogy’s creative achievement? Warner Bros will be hoping so, but has a tight window to present the film to voters, given a global release date of December 18. Star Timothée Chalamet has so far earned four Oscar nominations and six at Bafta, with no wins to date.

Elsinore Dir. Simon Stone Andrew Scott has been attracting strong awards buzz for his intense performance as the late Scottish actor Ian Charleson ever since Elsinore premiered at Telluride this summer. Scott has previously won TV and theatre awards, including a supporting actor Bafta for Sherlock in 2012, but has never been nominated for a film Bafta or Oscar. Scott and Elsinore writer Stephen Beresford collaborated on Pride , which won outstanding British film at the 2015 Baftas. Focus Features begins the US rollout on November 20, with Studiocanal to follow in the UK in January.

Fatherland Dir. Pawel Pawlikowski Mubi released the black-and-white, German-language drama across North America and the UK in October, and will hope for an awards run similar to Polish British director Pawlikowski’s last two, Ida (2013) and Cold War (2018). Ida won a Bafta and Oscar, and Cold War earned three nominations at both awards. Hanns Zischler and Sandra Hüller play novelist Thomas Mann and his daughter Erika travelling across 1949 Germany. Fatherland shared Cannes’ director prize with La Bola Negra and is Poland’s Oscar entry. Awards attention could also fall on cinematographer Lukasz Zal, nominated for two Oscars and a Bafta for Pawlikowski films.
Source: Neon
‘Fjord’

Fjord Dir. Cristian Mungiu In May, Romanian writer/director Mungiu collected his second Palme d’Or from Cannes, following his 2007 triumph 4 Months, 3 Weeks And 2 Days , for this debate-starting drama. Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve portray the heads of a conservative religious family who run afoul of a progressive Norwegian community that recoils from their parenting style. US distributor Neon, which has picked up rights for the past seven Palme d’Or winners, has collected the best picture Oscar twice during that span (with Parasite and Anora ). Fjord is Romania’s Oscar entry for international feature.

The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth Dir. David Fincher In 2020, Quentin Tarantino’s Once Upon A Time In Hollywood received 10 Oscar nominations, winning for production design and Brad Pitt’s supporting performance. This stand­alone sequel, written by Tarantino and directed by Fincher, is set in 1977, eight years after the events of the earlier film, and follows Pitt’s titular character who has transitioned from stuntman to studio fixer. Netflix releases exclusively at more than 500 Imax screens globally on November 25, and begins streaming on December 23. It will play a handful of smaller theatres, including Tarantino’s own New Beverly, in 35mm.

links.text: The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth

blocks.text: Godzilla Minus Zero Dir. Takashi Yamazaki Toho’s Godzilla Minus One caught global attention in 2023, grossing $57m in North America, $48m in Japan and $114m worldwide. Then the Japanese-language film, set just after the Second World War, crashed the awards party, vanquishing major US studio titles to win the visual effects Oscar with a VFX team led by director/writer Yamazaki. This 1949-set sequel sees war-torn Japan menaced by a new dragon-like creature — Godzilla to the rescue? The film is distributed by Toho-owned Gkids in the US and Anime Ltd in the UK.

I Play Rocky Dir. Peter Farrelly John Avildsen’s Rocky was a crowdpleasing underdog tale that resonated with audiences, going on to earn 10 Oscar nominations in 1977, and three wins including best picture. Farrelly’s I Play Rocky from Amazon MGM Studios is likewise a crowdpleasing underdog tale, this time telling the unlikely story of how struggling actor/screenwriter Sylvester Stallone (Anthony Ippolito) battled to play the lead in his own boxing drama. Farrelly’s Green Book beat fancied competitors including Roma to scoop the best picture Oscar in 2019, and Mahershala Ali won for supporting actor. Can history repeat?

Ink Dir. Danny Boyle Venice opener Ink , which also played Toronto and BFI London Film Festival, begins in 1969 as up-and-coming Australian media magnate Rupert Murdoch (Guy Pearce) recruits Larry Lamb (Jack O’Connell) to edit and turn around the fortunes of UK newspaper The Sun , with Lamb slapping sex and celebrity across the front page. Claire Foy — Bifa-nominated here for supporting performance — also stars. Ink heads to Netflix after a limited theatrical release in the US in December, and Studiocanal releases in the UK in January. Boyle’s awards haul includes the directing Oscar and Bafta for Slumdog Millionaire in 2009.

The Invite Dir. Olivia Wilde Released in early summer in the UK and US, this indie comedy — adapted from Cesc Gay’s 2020 Spanish film The People Upstairs — grossed more than $60m globally, with a reported budget of less than $15m. The warm reception started at Sundance, where A24 reportedly paid around $12m for North American rights to the Wilde-directed screwball comedy about an unhappy San Francisco couple (Wilde, Seth Rogen) who invite their liberated neighbours (Penelope Cruz, Ed Norton) for dinner. Awards voters will likely focus on the cast, Wilde’s directing, Will McCormack and Rashida Jones’ adapted screenplay and the picture overall.

Iron Boy Dir. Louis Clichy The first solo-directed feature from Pixar alumnus Clichy represents a change of style from his work as an animator on the likes of Up and WALL·E . Set in rural north France, semi-autobiographical coming-of‑age tale Iron Boy ( Le Corset ) offers a pleasing combination of watercolour wash plus hand-drawn pen-and-ink 2D animation. Following a Cannes Un Certain Regard premiere where it picked up a special jury prize, the film played in competition at Annecy, carrying off the audience and jury awards. Sony Pictures Classics releases in the US, with Picturehouse Entertainment following in the UK. In France, KMBO had achieved 408,000 admissions for the film at press time.
Source: Sundance Film Festival
‘Josephine’

Josephine Dir. Beth de Araujo For her second feature, de Araujo ( Soft & Quiet ) drew inspiration from a traumatic childhood incident, telling the story of a young girl (Mason Reeves) who tries to process a violent sexual assault she witnesses in the park. Taking home the grand jury and audience prizes in the US Dramatic Competition at Sundance — a feat similarly achieved by awards-season darlings CODA in 2021 and Minari in 2020 — Josephine stars Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan as the girl’s worried, feuding parents. The film also recently earned three Gotham Awards nods, for best feature, supporting performance for Tatum and breakthrough performer for Reeves. Sumerian Pictures releases in the US and Curzon in the UK, both on November 20.

La Bola Negra Dirs. Javier Ambrossi, Javier Calvo The buzzy second feature from the Spanish directing duo known as Los Javis is an ambitious, multi-­stranded, gay-themed epic. It has been gathering momentum since premiering in Cannes Competition, where it shared the directing prize with Fatherland and saw Netflix swoop on North American rights. Adding Toronto’s People’s Choice award to its prize haul elevated the Spanish domestic box-office smash from favourite in the international feature line-up to a serious contender in other categories, including best picture and supporting actor for musician Guitarricadelafuente. Altitude released in the UK in early November, opening with $710,000 (£536,000) from 113 sites.

La Gradiva Dir. Marine Atlan César-nominated French cinematographer Atlan made a splash in Cannes with her second feature as director (following 2018’s Daniel ), winning the Critics’ Week grand prize for this tale of French high-school seniors on a trip to Naples and the ruins of Pompeii. Four Gotham nominations followed, and La Gradiva competes with La Bola Negra , Club Kid , All Of A Sudden and Possible Love in the British Independent Film Awards’ ultra-­competitive international category. 1-2 Special releases in the US, and Metis Films in the UK, making the drama eligible for Oscar and Bafta.

A Long Winter Dir. Andrew Haigh Haigh adapts a short story by Irish novelist Colm Toibin for this quiet 1950s period piece about a fractured Colorado family living in the Rocky mountains. Haigh’s All Of Us Strangers won seven Bifas in 2023, going on to earn six nominations at the 2024 Baftas. Awards attention is likely to focus on his direction, his adapted screenplay and the performances of an ensemble centred on Fred Hechinger, Caitriona Balfe and Ebon Moss-Bachrach. Shot in Alberta, Mubi co-­financed the atmospheric slow-burner with Film4 and will release it in December in the US and January in the UK.
Source: Glen Wilson / Lionsgate
‘Michael’

Michael Dir. Antoine Fuqua Michael could follow the trajectory achieved by Bohemian Rhapsody , also from producer Graham King. The Freddie Mercury biopic was initially underestimated as an awards contender, going on to win two Baftas and four Oscars, including lead actor at both for Rami Malek; Fuqua also directed Denzel Washington to a 2002 Oscar in Training Day . Jaafar Jackson takes on the difficult challenge of singing, dancing and acting just like his uncle Michael, while Colman Domingo impresses as overbearing patriarch and manager Joseph Jackson.

Minotaur Dir. Andrey Zvyagintsev Much has happened in the life of the now-dissident Russian director since his last film Loveless in 2017. He survived a life-threatening Covid-related illness and, as a vocal opponent of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, was forced to relocate from Russia to France. This Cannes grand prix-­winning crime drama, France’s pick for the international feature Oscar, represents a filmmaker whose gift for trenchant sociopolitical commentary is undiminished. Following Oscar and Bafta nominations for both Loveless and Leviathan , the film’s US and UK distributor Mubi will hope Minotaur makes for third time lucky for Zvyagintsev.

Misty Green Dir. Chris Rock US comedian and actor Rock’s fourth directorial outing marks his first serious foray into the awards conversation (he has twice hosted the Oscars ceremony, in 2005 and 2016). The film, which world premiered in Toronto and also played BFI London Film Festival, follows a Los Angeles actress whose star has been dimmed by industry racism, sexism and her own self-­destruction. A standout performance from UK lead Rosalind Eleazar could ignite voter attention. Daniel Kaluuya, Adam Driver and Anna Kendrick also star. A24 gave Misty Green a limited US theatrical release ahead of landing on Netflix, and also released in the UK.

Obsession Dir. Curry Barker After premiering in Toronto’s Midnight Madness section in 2025, this micro-budget horror film was acquired by Focus Features and became a sleeper sensation, grossing $525m worldwide. Breakout star Inde Navarrette, playing a woman trapped in a spell that makes her fall dangerously in love with her friend (Michael Johnston), hopes to follow in the footsteps of Weapons ’ Amy Madigan, who turned an acclaimed horror performance into an Oscar win. Barker could receive recognition for his original screenplay, after Jordan Peele ( Get Out ) and Ryan Coogler ( Sinners ) demonstrated that auteur-driven genre hits can resonate with voters.

The Odyssey Dir. Christopher Nolan Nolan’s last blockbuster Oppenheimer grossed $976m worldwide and won seven Oscars and seven Baftas, with the writer/­director collecting two prizes from each organisation for best picture and directing. Can The Odyssey match or even exceed those numbers? Nolan’s adaptation of the epic Homer poem has already bested his previous picture at the box office, earning $1.8bn to date. Matt Damon and Anne Hathaway star in a Universal release that looks to be a serious contender in major categories, with previous winners — cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema, editor Jennifer Lame and composer Ludwig Göransson — all in play as well.

Paper Tiger Dir. James Gray US filmmaker Gray directs a starry cast including Adam Driver, Scarlett Johansson and Miles Teller for this moody 1980s-set morality tale taking place in Queens, New York City. It tells the story of two brothers — one an ex-cop (Driver), the other a family-­focused engineer (Teller) — whose business plans fall foul of the Russian mafia. Gray has yet to receive an Oscar or Bafta nomination, while Johansson and Driver have notched up several nominations apiece, and Johansson won a best actress Bafta for Lost In Translation in 2004. Neon picked up US and UK rights ahead of the film’s Cannes Competition debut.

Possible Love Dir. Lee Chang-dong Lee’s satisfyingly weighty drama about the complex relationships and tricky power dynamics between two married couples picked up the grand jury prize Silver Lion following its premiere at Venice. It is South Korea’s submission for the international feature Oscar, and director Lee’s fourth film to represent the country in the category — following Burning , Secret Sunshine and Oasis — and his strongest shot yet at making it beyond the shortlist of 15. Netflix gave the film a theatrical push and began streaming in early November.

Primetime Dir. Lance Oppenheim Oppenheim has major awards heat as director of You Can See Everything alongside Nathan Fielder, so could that mean voters sideline his biographical drama Primetime , starring Robert Pattinson as To Catch A Predator presenter Chris Hansen? The A24 film has been a profitable hit with North American audiences ($62m at press time), while performances from Pattinson, Skyler Gisondo and Merritt Wever are admired. David Osit’s documentary Predators , telling the story of the NBC sting-operation series, was part of the awards conver­sation last year, but struck out at Oscar and Bafta.

Project Hail Mary Dirs. Phil Lord, Christopher Miller Released in March, Amazon MGM Studios’ crowdpleasing adaptation of Andy Weir’s sci-fi novel grossed $685m worldwide. Project Hail Mary now sets its sights on awards season, with Ryan Gosling a contender as a high-school science teacher on an interstellar mission to save Earth. Directors Lord and Miller have won one animation Oscar ( Spider-Man: Into The Spider-Verse ) and two Baftas (including The Lego Movie ), and cinematographer Greig Fraser won the Oscar and Bafta for 2021’s Dune . Holly­wood’s previous Weir adaptation The Martian was also a hit with voters, garnering seven Oscar nominations and six Bafta nods in 2016.

Ray Gunn Dir. Brad Bird A long-cherished project from double Oscar winner Bird ( The Incredibles , Ratatouille ), Ray Gunn is a noir-infused retro-futurist animation with an array of acknowledged influences from The Maltese Falcon to Buck Rogers . The eponymous hero is a wise-cracking 1940s-style private detective, with a three-legged monocular alien sidekick. The handsomely realised Art Deco-inspired backdrop of this Net­flix-­backed picture, complete with flying cars, jet packs and — naturally — ray guns, will likely catch the eye of voters. Wild Horse Nine ’s Sam Rockwell leads the voice cast, alongside Scarlett Johansson and Tom Waits.
Source: Schubert,ROW Pictures,Walker+Worm Film,Gerald_Kerkletz
‘Rose’

Rose Dir. Markus Schleinzer Sandra Hüller is in contention for acting awards with both Fatherland and Project Hail Mary , but this could be her best shot — Austrian director Schleinzer’s black-and-white drama set in the 17th century. Hüller won the leading performance Silver Bear at the Berlinale, where Rose launched, playing a woman who has taken on a male identity while claiming to be the long-missing heir to a neglected estate. This third feature from Schleinzer has been chosen as Austria’s entry to the international feature Oscar, and is distributed by Mubi in the US and UK.

Sense And Sensibility Dir. Georgia Oakley Blue Jean director Oakley earned praise for her fresh take on the Austen classic, leaning into the Dashwood sisters’ kinship with nature after their family relocates to relatively humble lodgings in Devonshire. Bafta’s outstanding British film category seems the likeliest path to a nomination for the Working Title Films production/Focus Features release. Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles lead the cast — playing the siblings whose contrasting natures are suggested by the title — while Fiona Shaw shines as the gossipy, gleefully unpretentious Mrs Jennings.

Shaun The Sheep: The Beast Of Mossy Bottom Dirs. Steve Cox, Matthew Walker Aardman’s Shaun The Sheep Movie was nominated for animated feature at Bafta and Oscar in 2016, and 2019’s A Shaun The Sheep Movie: Farmageddon achieved the exact same double feat. This giddy threequel — which sees Farmer accidentally fall victim to a scientific experiment cooked up by Shaun — keeps the clever, witty moments on maximum flow, and has every chance of endearing the stop-motion caper to voters all over again. Gkids released in the US, and Studiocanal for Sky Cinema in the UK, with UK and Ireland box office standing at $7.8m (£5.9m) at press time.

links.text: Shaun The Sheep: The Beast Of Mossy Bottom

blocks.text: Tangles Dir. Leah Nelson Sarah Leavitt’s autobiographical graphic novel, which threads together her own queer coming-of-age with the challenge of her mother’s early-onset dementia, is adapted by Nelson into a punky, affecting animation. Following its Cannes premiere, Tangles has picked up a slew of prizes at festivals such as Deauville and San Sebastian. High-profile voice talent — including Julia Louis-­Dreyfus, Seth Rogen and Bryan Cranston — could help put this predominantly black-and-white 2D animation on the radar of voters. IFC’s late-November Academy run in the US precedes a January release.

Teenage Sex And Death At Camp Miasma Dir. Jane Schoenbrun Schoenbrun’s fourth feature, a knowing indie horror that explores queer identity and stars Hannah Einbinder and Gillian Anderson, premiered in Cannes’ Un Certain Regard where it won the Queer Palm. The US filmmaker’s past films, especially 2024’s I Saw The TV Glow , have been garlanded by festivals and critics but eluded the attention of major awards bodies. Three nominations in this year’s Gotham Awards — for Schoenbrun, Anderson and the film overall — start the film’s awards season with a bang. Mubi financed the reported $10m production, and released in the US and UK in August.

links.text: Teenage Sex And Death At Camp Miasma

blocks.text: Tender Loving Care Dir. Mike Leigh The 17th theatrical feature from UK veteran Leigh was co-financed by Film4 and Bleecker Street, and launched at Telluride. The London-­set comic drama explores the relationships between a social worker (Kate O’Flynn), her flatmate (Alice Bailey Johnson) and her parents (Marion Bailey, Paul Jesson). Leigh, who has said this will be his last film, has been Oscar-nominated seven times and never won, although he has won several Baftas plus the top prizes at Cannes and Venice. Bleecker Street opens the film in the US in December, with Studiocanal following in the UK in February.
Source: Apple TV
‘Tenzing’

Tenzing Dir. Jennifer Peedom Having directed the 2015 Bafta-­nominated documentary Sherpa , Australia’s Peedom returns again to the slopes of Everest, this time for a stirring biographical drama about Sherpa Tenzing Norgay. The film premiered in Telluride and later picked up the audience award at Mill Valley Film Festival. Genden Phuntsok impresses in the title role, while Tom Hiddleston as Tenzing’s climbing partner Edmund Hillary is also in the mix for nominations. Likewise in contention in this crowdpleasing Apple TV production is Stefan Duscio for the film’s arresting cinematography.

Toy Story 5 Dir. Andrew Stanton The fifth film in Pixar’s beloved computer-animated series sees Jessie the cowgirl take centre stage in a story that taps into parents’ mounting anxiety about screen time and authentic play. The film touched a nerve: with a box office of $1.15bn worldwide, it is the highest-grossing film of the Toy Story series and currently ranks third at the 2026 global box office after Spider-Man: Brand New Day and The Odyssey . Nominations in animation categories are likely; the film is also favoured to earn a nod for best original song, for Taylor Swift’s ‘I Knew It, I Knew You’.

Werwulf Dir. Robert Eggers Eggers’ latest elevated genre tale arrives two years after his similarly colour-desaturated Nosferatu , which earned $182m at the worldwide box office and a decent haul of craft nominations at Bafta and Oscar. Likewise from Focus Features, and with returning cast members including Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Lily-Rose Depp and Willem Dafoe, gothic folk horror Werwulf is set in 14th-­century England as the countryside is haunted by a beast. Cinematographer Jarin Blaschke, composer Robin Carolan and production designer Craig Lathrop are among the returning HoDs.

Wild Horse Nine Dir. Martin McDonagh Celebrated playwright McDonagh’s fifth feature received stellar reviews out of its Venice premiere, and Searchlight Pictures hopes it will be his third straight picture to be nominated for the top prize at Oscar and Bafta, following Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri and The Banshees Of Inisherin (with Three Billboards winning the best film Bafta in 2018). This 1973-set comedy thriller stars John Malkovich, who is heavily favoured to be nominated — his last Oscar/Bafta nod was for In The Line Of Fire in 1994 — and Sam Rockwell, who won the Oscar and Bafta best supporting actor awards for Three Billboards .

Wildwood Dir. Travis Night Some 15 years in the making, Laika’s epic stop-motion animated fantasy adventure is adapted from the 2011 novel by Colin Meloy and Carson Ellis. The scale, scope and intricacy of Wildwood ’s action setpieces help make it one of the titles to beat in an unusually strong year for animated features. Elsewhere, this US Fathom release (and via Black Bear in the UK) could also earn nods for original song with ‘The Better Part Of Bravery’ by The Decemberists, and for Dario Marianelli’s score. A cinematography nod for Caleb Deschanel is not out of the question.

Woman Unknown Dir. May el-Toukhy El-Toukhy’s Venice Golden Lion-winning drama is a restrained but quietly devastating study of a woman’s desperation. It is set in Denmark in the aftermath of the Second World War, and follows a young nanny and housemaid (Mathilde Arcel) who is about to marry her widowed employer. Woman Unknown is Denmark’s submission for the international feature Oscar, which was picked up at the recent AFM by Cohen Media for US distribution. In the UK, the film’s March 2027 release by Vue Lumière is within the extended window permitted by Bafta for films not in the English language.

Wuthering Heights Dir. Emerald Fennell Fennell follows Promising Young Woman and Saltburn with her first film based on existing source material, putting her distinctive directorial stamp on Emily Brontë’s Yorkshire Moors-set tortured romance. The filmmaker certainly succeeded in engaging audiences, achieving $33.2m (£25.3m) at the UK and Ireland box office, $84m in North America and $242m worldwide. Lead actors Margot Robbie and Jacob Elordi have so far racked up more nominations at Bafta than Oscar, while Fennell has two Bafta wins and one Oscar (all for Promising Young Woman ).

You Can See Everything Dirs. Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim Documentaries rarely impact the best picture Oscar race — no nonfiction film has ever received a nomination — but that could change with A24’s zeitgeisty portrait of controversial Theranos CEO Elizabeth Holmes. Since its top-secret Telluride premiere, the film has grossed a remarkable $79m in the US to date. Four-time Primetime Emmy Award nominee Fielder makes his feature-length directing debut, while Oppenheim is also in the awards conversation for Primetime . And a certain actress with a connection to this subject could be a surprise contender for playing Holmes in the film’s reconstruction segments.

Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother Dir. Bassam Tariq Two-time supporting actor Oscar winner Mahershala Ali ( Moonlight , Green Book ) looks set to drum up noise in the leading category as a Muslim Texan whose days moonlighting as a contract killer look numbered after a family tragedy — only to be called up for one final job. The Amazon MGM actioner played Toronto and BFI London film festivals ahead of a US theatrical run, grossing $3.6m. Tariq was Bafta-nominated in 2021 for feature debut Mogul Mowgli . Babak Anvari, a Bafta winner for his feature directing debut Under The Shadow , is among the producers.

blocks.text: 10 performances to tempt voters
Source: Bleecker Street
The Liberation

Emily Blunt - Disclosure Day Sci-fi thriller Disclosure Day returned Spielberg to a broader commercial mainstream after his forays into musicals ( West Side Story ) and personal biography ( The Fabelmans ), grossing $248m worldwide. Blunt won plaudits as a TV weather presenter who teams up with Josh O’Connor’s cyber­security expert, unravelling mysteries of their own past while on a mission to disclose the truth about alien life on Earth. Blunt has four Bafta film nominations and one at Oscar.

Joan Collins - My Duchess Scripted by Louise Fennell, directed by Mike Newell, and from an original idea by its star Collins, My Duchess recounts the years in the life of Wallis Simpson after the 1972 death of the former King Edward VIII, with Isabella Rossellini as the forceful lawyer who asserts control — to Wallis’s detriment. The zippy melodrama veers entertainingly into What Ever Happened To Baby Jane? territory, while Collins enjoys a rich arc from spirited dowager to abused elder.

Carrie Coon - The Liberation Coon has been in the film awards conversation before with His Three Daughters (2023) and The Nest (2020), but has never achieved a Bafta or Oscar nomination. This time, she competes via Guy Nattiv’s Telluride-launched drama about a woman drawn to a cult-like commune. Distributor Bleecker Street is campaigning the film in the US; UK distribution (and thus Bafta eligibility) remained a question mark at press time.

Monica Dolan - The Lost Children Of Tuam Dolan makes a sparky contribution to Elsinore and is also in Parkinson’s-­themed UK indie Onwards And Sideways , but she impresses most playing real-life amateur local historian Catherine Corless. In 2014, she made front-page news in Ireland with research into a former mother-and-baby home in her local town, where hundreds of improper infant burials had occurred. The Galway Film Fleadh premiere had grossed $688,000 (£522,000) in UK and Ireland cinemas at press time.

Cynthia Erivo - Prima Facie Suzie Miller’s 2019 one-woman play Prima Facie was memorably staged in a London West End production starring Jodie Comer, and the NT Live filmed version grossed an amazing $12m (£9m) in UK and Ireland cinemas. Susanna White’s feature film version leans on Cynthia Erivo’s admired turn as an ambitious barrister who successfully defends men accused of sex crimes, and then herself becoming the victim of one. Sony released in US and UK on November 13, following festival play at Toronto and BFI London.

Helen Mirren - A Talent For Murder Joanna Murray-Smith’s 2014 stageplay Switzerland is adapted by the writer for the big screen, directed by Anton Corbijn and released in the US by Bleecker Street. Mirren plays reclusive author Patricia Highsmith, toying with Alden Ehrenreich’s junior literary editor despatched to persuade her to write another Tom Ripley book. The actress has several Oscar and Bafta nominations, winning both in 2007 for The Queen .

Dominic Sessa - Tony A summer in the life of future celebrity chef and author Anthony Bourdain — perhaps a relatively lightweight contender for awards glory, but one appreciated by audiences, who propelled Matt Johnson’s film to a $19m global box office. Sessa, who was Bafta-­nominated for The Holdovers in 2024 but passed over for Oscar, shines in another coming-of-age role, while Leo Woodall mines his sexy bad boy persona again to entertaining effect.

Léa Seydoux - Gentle Monster Seydoux was a joint winner of the Palme d’Or (alongside director Abdellatif Kechiche and co-star Adele Exarchopoulos) at Cannes in 2013 for Blue Is The Warmest Colour and a Bafta rising star nominee in 2014. This year she could catch awards attention in Marie Kreutzer’s Gentle Monster as a concert pianist (and wife and mother) whose husband is accused of possessing child pornography. Netflix has rights in several English-­speaking markets including the US and UK.

Jeremy Strong - The Social Reckoning Written and directed by Aaron Sorkin, this is a standalone follow-up to David Fincher and Sorkin’s 2010 hit The Social Network , winner of three Oscars and three Baftas. Sorkin’s whistleblower drama has not achieved equivalent critical and box-office impact, but voters may enjoy Strong as a graceless Mark Zuckerberg, seemingly reframing the Meta chairman and CEO as a product of functional autism.

John Turturro - The Only Living Pickpocket In New York Rian Johnson and Ram Bergman’s T-Street is the production company behind this US indie from writer/director Noah Segan, an actor who has had roles in six Johnson/Bergman films. Turturro breathes humanity into his New York City pickpocket role, racing across multiple boroughs in a bid to lessen the damage after stealing a crypto currency wallet from the wrong guy. Sony Pictures Classics released in October.
